sentences.text: Charonosaurus was a very large hadrosaur estimated to be around 10 meters in length and 5 metric tons in body mass.
This animal likely possessed a long, backward-projecting hollow crest similar to Parasaurolophus, supported by highly modified frontal bones.
The femur of Charonosaurus could reach 1.35 meters in length, longer than any other known hadrosaur of its time except Shantungosaurus giganteus.
Adult Charonosaurus had approximately 40 rows of teeth in the lower jaw, with only one to two teeth in use at a time, and the dental crowns reached up to 40 millimeters in height.
The sacrum of Charonosaurus consisted of nine fused vertebrae.
The genus name Charonosaurus is derived from Charon, the Greek mythological ferryman of the dead, and the Greek word for lizard.
The specific epithet jiayinensis refers to the type locality, the site of Jiayin.

Fossils of Charonosaurus were discovered in 1975 near the city of Jiayin in the Amur region, and the species was formally described in 2000 based on a partial skull housed at the University of Science and Technology of Changchun. These fossils were originally described by Anatoly Riabinin as Mandschurosaurus amurensis and a fragmentary hadrosaur ischium as Saurolophus krystofovici, but both names are now considered nomina dubia. The holotype was designated CUST J-V1251-57 by Pascal Godefroit, Shuqin Zan, and Liyong Jin.
The orientation of long bones suggests they were transported and deposited by a river.
Abundant ejected teeth from carnivorous dinosaurs found in the bone beds suggest Charonosaurus carcasses were consumed by predators and scavengers or that the animals were killed during river hunts.
Charonosaurus belongs to the family Hadrosauridae and is classified in the class Ornithischia.

A 2000 cladistic analysis based on skull, teeth, and postcranial features shows Charonosaurus jiayinensis is most closely related to Parasaurolophus among Lambeosaurinae, and within the subfamily Lambeosaurinae, Charonosaurus and Parasaurolophus are closely related in the tribe Parasaurolophini. The parent group of Charonosaurus is Parasaurolophini.
The genus is a monotypic genus consisting only of the species C. jiayinensis.

Charonosaurus lived during the Late Cretaceous, between approximately 69.9 and 66 million years ago, in what is now Asia. It also lived during the Maastrichtian stage, between 72.2 and 66 million years ago.
Charonosaurus indicates that lambeosaurines survived until the end of the Cretaceous, a time when this group is not known from North America.

There is an ongoing debate regarding the exact phylogenetic placement of Charonosaurus, with different studies yielding conflicting results. A 2021 study by Ramírez-Velasco et al. placed Charonosaurus closer to Tlatolophus and Blasisaurus than to Parasaurolophus.
